1.pericope_label: Now it came to pass in the seventh month, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah the son of Elishama, of the seed royal, and the princes of the king, even ten men with him, came unto Gedaliah the son of Ahikam to Mizpah; and there they did eat bread together in Mizpah. Then arose Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the ten men that were with him, and smote Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan with the sword, and slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land. Ishmael also slew all the Jews that were with him, even with Gedaliah, at Mizpah, and the Chaldeans that were found there, and the men of war.

schools.summary: Ellicott reconstructs the visit as one of courtesy and recognition, possibly timed for the feast, compares the treachery to a modern massacre of a host by his guests, and raises and answers the difficulty of how ten men killed so many; Keil and Delitzsch restrict the slaughter from the wording to those present in the house and the guard allowed him, weigh a proposed emendation of one verb, and read the added clause as the narrator's own reflection on the greatness of the crime.

Gill collects three rival datings and the fast afterwards kept on the occasion, and declines the historian's larger account of a night massacre through the city on the ground that the people were afterwards carried off captive; Calvin makes the violated hospitality the heart of the crime, noting that even the heathen counted its breach the greatest atrocity, and traces the motive to a royal descent whose high notions its holder would not relinquish.

Clarke names the month, supplies the custom that eating bread together was the same as a solemn covenant, and refers the killing back to the preceding chapter; Wesley measures three months from the fall of the city and notes that the royal blood both raised the murderer's spirits and made him a fitter instrument for the foreign king.

Henry finds scarcely such an instance of perfidious cruelty in all of scripture, stresses the artifice by which friendship was pretended and no warning given, and reads the whole as permitted for the completing of the ruin of an unhumbled people.

debates.question: On what day did the murder happen?

positions.position: On the third of the seventh month, fifty-two days after the temple's destruction; though some put it on the first day, and a historian dates it thirty days after the warning.
Three months after the capture of the city.
In the seventh month, answering to the first new moon of October.
Only those present in the house, and of the soldiers only the guard allowed him; the wording shows as much.
Only those who resisted or might have avenged the governor, since the main body were afterwards carried off captive.
Perhaps no wider than the guests, who may have been surprised unarmed at meat, each of the ten princes possibly having brought a retinue.
All found in arms, whether of their own nation or the conquerors, and all in any capacity to avenge the death.

outliers.claim: Traces the murder to the pride of a royal descent already broken, observing that those once in any dignity can hardly relinquish the high notions that inflate them, so that reduced to extreme want they still aim at something royal and never submit to the power of God.

themes: Now it came to pass in the seventh month, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah the son of Elishama, of the seed royal, and the princes of the king, even ten men with him, came unto Gedaliah the son of Ahikam to Mizpah; and there they did eat bread together in Mizpah.

Then arose Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the ten men that were with him, and smote Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan with the sword, and slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.
Ishmael also slew all the Jews that were with him, even with Gedaliah, at Mizpah, and the Chaldeans that were found there, and the men of war.

4.pericope_label: And it came to pass the second day after he had slain Gedaliah, and no man knew it, That there came certain from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from Samaria, even fourscore men, having their beards shaven, and their clothes rent, and having cut themselves, with offerings and incense in their hand, to bring them to the house of the Lord. And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah went forth from Mizpah to meet them, weeping all along as he went: and it came to pass, as he met them, he said unto them, Come to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam.

schools.summary: Ellicott records that the old Greek gives a different second place-name suiting the order better, notes that the pilgrims carried the meat offering rather than burnt offerings, criticises their mourning signs as a relapse into a custom the law forbade, and adds that the Greek makes the pilgrims rather than their host the weepers; Keil and Delitzsch keep to the road and the topography and give the killing plainly.

Gill places the three home towns in the northern kingdom and reconstructs the calculation behind the meeting on the road; Calvin rejects as an incredible evasion the answer that the pilgrims had not heard of the burning, holds that they came knowingly to testify their piety where they had formerly sacrificed, and finds no motive for the second murder beyond the principle that wicked men set no bounds once begun.

Clarke takes the mourning signs as ordinary in those countries and reads the weeping on the road as the performance of a felonious hypocrite, supplying the bait about vineyards and fields; Wesley supposes the pilgrims had not heard the temple was burnt and limits the general ignorance to those living at a distance.

debates.question: Did the pilgrims know the temple had been destroyed?

positions.position: No: they had probably not heard of it.
Yes: that answer is an incredible evasion, since the burning was two months earlier and they came from places near at hand; they brought no victims but came to testify their piety at the site.
They came as mourners to the ruins, perhaps hoping to find at least an altar standing.

debates.question: What do the shaven beards and rent clothes signify?

positions.position: Ordinary signs of deep mourning in those countries, probably for the destruction of the city.
Marks of a particular occasion, and in themselves a relapse into a half-heathen custom the law had forbidden.

outliers.claim: Records that the old Greek text makes the pilgrims, and not the man who met them, the ones who were weeping as they went.

themes: And it came to pass the second day after he had slain Gedaliah, and no man knew it,

That there came certain from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from Samaria, even fourscore men, having their beards shaven, and their clothes rent, and having cut themselves, with offerings and incense in their hand, to bring them to the house of the Lord.
And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah went forth from Mizpah to meet them, weeping all along as he went: and it came to pass, as he met them, he said unto them, Come to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam.

7.pericope_label: And it was so, when they came into the midst of the city, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah slew them, and cast them into the midst of the pit, he, and the men that were with him. But ten men were found among them that said unto Ishmael, Slay us not: for we have treasures in the field, of wheat, and of barley, and of oil, and of honey. So he forbare, and slew them not among their brethren. Now the pit wherein Ishmael had cast all the dead bodies of the men, whom he had slain because of Gedaliah, was it which Asa the king had made for fear of Baasha king of Israel: and Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with them that were slain.

schools.summary: Ellicott admits the purpose of the second murder does not appear and offers four possible motives, explains the hidden stores as the previous year's produce concealed during the occupation, gives the fortress history behind the pit and two accounts of what it was, and records a variant reading of the phrase naming the murdered governor; Keil and Delitzsch describe the subterranean granaries whose entrances a stranger's eye could not find and note that such places are still in use.

Gill adds from the historian that the court was shut on the pilgrims as they entered; Calvin reads the sparing of ten as avarice overcoming ferocity, so that many monsters were in one man, guesses that want of provisions made him moderate, asks why God suffered mourners to fall as prey to robbers, and reasons that a pit in the middle of a city was probably an inner citadel of refuge.

Clarke reconstructs the plan by which the eighty were decoyed so that there would be strength enough to kill them, gives the local name for the underground granaries, and doubts the ten were spared for long once the treasures were in hand; Wesley states the whole motive briefly, that covetousness prevailed over cruelty.

positions.position: The motive does not appear: their presence may have roused bitterness, their recognition of the governor may have looked like treachery, or the deed may have been retaliation or plunder.
No motive can be found; once a man has polluted his hands he makes no end of his barbarity.
They were decoyed so that the murderer would have strength enough to kill them and keep the first murder secret.

debates.question: What was the pit that the bodies were cast into?

positions.position: A reservoir made to supply the fortified town with water during the old war.
Either a defensive trench with a drawbridge, or one of the tanks made to supply a fortress.
Probably an inner citadel of refuge, since this one lay in the middle of the city.

outliers.claim: Raises the question why God suffered men who had left their homes to lament the burning of the temple to fall as prey to robbers, and answers only that God has hidden ways of providing for the safety of his people.

themes: And it was so, when they came into the midst of the city, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah slew them, and cast them into the midst of the pit, he, and the men that were with him.

But ten men were found among them that said unto Ishmael, Slay us not: for we have treasures in the field, of wheat, and of barley, and of oil, and of honey. So he forbare, and slew them not among their brethren.

Now the pit wherein Ishmael had cast all the dead bodies of the men, whom he had slain because of Gedaliah, was it which Asa the king had made for fear of Baasha king of Israel: and Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with them that were slain.

10.pericope_label: Then Ishmael carried away captive all the residue of the people that were in Mizpah, even the king’s daughters, and all the people that remained in Mizpah, whom Nebuzar–adan the captain of the guard had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam: and Ishmael the son of Nethaniah carried them away captive, and departed to go over to the Ammonites. But when Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces that were with him, heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done, Then they took all the men, and went to fight with Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and found him by the great waters that are in Gibeon.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the seizure of the princesses as a dynastic claim asserted after the fashion of the East, notes the earlier alliance that promised a refuge, and describes the pool by its remains and its earlier history while setting aside the historian's rival location as off the route; Keil and Delitzsch identify the same pool and infer from its nearness that the news travelled fast and the captains mustered quickly.

Gill limits the captives to the unarmed survivors and notes that the pursuers believed the report at once, having given the warning themselves; Calvin cannot decide whether the abduction was planned from the first, speculates about the foreign king's designs on the land, and raises two difficulties nobody else does, the force needed to gather a scattered people and the presence of royal daughters at all.
Clarke says simply that the captives were taken to be sold as slaves among the Ammonites.

Henry wishes the captains had stayed as a lifeguard instead of being away on some expedition, calls the pursuit an after-game, regrets that vengeance suffered the murderers to live, and observes that the most cruel are often the most cowardly.

debates.question: Why were the survivors carried off?

positions.position: To be sold as slaves among the Ammonites.
To assert a dynastic claim through the princesses and to secure a refuge with an allied king.
By a plan probably settled beforehand, the foreign king hoping to plant his own people and rule the land as tributary.
At the pool of the town two miles north, whose remains are still visible; the historian's placing of it far to the south would not lie on the route.
At waters called great as a common name, not because rains had lately made them abundant.

outliers.claim: Draws from the captives wheeling about to their rescuers the rule that those who would be helped must help themselves, and from the captains' absence that those who affect to ramble are often out of their place at the moment they are wanted.

themes: Then Ishmael carried away captive all the residue of the people that were in Mizpah, even the king’s daughters, and all the people that remained in Mizpah, whom Nebuzar–adan the captain of the guard had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam: and Ishmael the son of Nethaniah carried them away captive, and departed to go over to the Ammonites.
But when Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces that were with him, heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done,
Then they took all the men, and went to fight with Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and found him by the great waters that are in Gibeon.

13.pericope_label: Now it came to pass, that when all the people which were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces that were with him, then they were glad. So all the people that Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah cast about and returned, and went unto Johanan the son of Kareah. But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites.

schools.summary: Ellicott finds in the captives' gladness evidence of how popular the murdered governor had been, and infers from the eight survivors that two of the original ten perished in one or other of the conflicts; Keil and Delitzsch record the escape without comment and pass to its consequence.

Gill distinguishes the captives from the murderer's own men and describes the desertion as complete, and accounts for the eight by supposing two killed, taken, or fled another way; Calvin locates the cause in the balance of force, and then raises alone the question why the murderer was allowed to escape at all, answering that God prolongs the life of the wicked so that the punishment is not forgotten.
Clarke gives the captives' motive as weariness of a tyrant and gladness at an opportunity to abandon him.

debates.question: Why did the captives change sides?

positions.position: Weariness of the tyrant and gladness at the chance to abandon him.
Because they knew the rescuers to be friends who had come to deliver them, and no longer feared their captor's authority.
Because the murdered governor had been popular and they welcomed the prospect of his death being avenged.
Because the rescuers came sufficiently armed and were trained soldiers, so that their captor could not be equal to them.

outliers.claim: Answers why the murderer was suffered to escape by arguing that God prolongs the life of the most wicked so that a punishment executed suddenly may not be forgotten, setting them as in a theatre to be looked on at leisure, and finds the vengeance carried out in the disgrace of a fugitive arriving with eight men and no hope of return.

themes: Now it came to pass, that when all the people which were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces that were with him, then they were glad.
So all the people that Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah cast about and returned, and went unto Johanan the son of Kareah.
But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites.

16.pericope_label: Then took Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces that were with him, all the remnant of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, from Mizpah, after that he had slain Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, even mighty men of war, and the women, and the children, and the eunuchs, whom he had brought again from Gibeon: And they departed, and dwelt in the habitation of Chimham, which is by Beth–lehem, to go to enter into Egypt, Because of the Chaldeans: for they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had slain Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon made governor in the land.

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the survivors of the royal household and reconstructs the benefaction behind the resting-place, suggesting it was probably the same shelter as the inn of the Nativity, and gives the fear its reasonable ground, that punishment was likely without careful inquiry into who was guilty; Keil and Delitzsch derive the rare word for the lodging etymologically, adjudicate between two forms of the name in the copies, and tie the clause about the conquerors to the purpose of going into Egypt.

Gill notes that the captains did not think fit to pursue and that some would join the clause about the conquerors to the preceding verse; Calvin reads the terms describing the company as praise for courage before withdrawing it, and refuses to let the fear excuse the flight, since they might have sent to the conqueror, cleared themselves and obtained pardon.
Clarke assigns the women, children and eunuchs to the palace and harem of the last king and takes the resting-place as a mere halt on a journey already resolved upon.

debates.question: What was the habitation they stopped at?

positions.position: The estate given to the son of the Gileadite chief, taken merely as a resting-place.
A caravanserai founded by that son out of gratitude for the patrimony bestowed on him, probably the same shelter as the inn of the Nativity.
A lodging or caravanserai, the word occurring only here; the marginal form of the founder's name is the correct one.

debates.question: Was the flight into Egypt excusable?

positions.position: The fear was well grounded, since punishment was likely without careful inquiry, and remaining with the murderer might be read as evidence of complicity.
The fear was not without reason but excuses nothing: they might have sent to the conqueror, thrown the blame on the guilty man and obtained pardon.

outliers.claim: Judges the rescuing captain in advance of the next chapter, that though energetic and mindful of the public good he betrayed his unbelief by leading the remnant into Egypt against the prophet's word, so that the chief thing, piety and the fear of God, was wanting in him.

themes: Then took Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces that were with him, all the remnant of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, from Mizpah, after that he had slain Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, even mighty men of war, and the women, and the children, and the eunuchs, whom he had brought again from Gibeon:
And they departed, and dwelt in the habitation of Chimham, which is by Beth–lehem, to go to enter into Egypt,
Because of the Chaldeans: for they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had slain Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon made governor in the land.
